title: Proof pages for a small consultancy
metaTitle: Proof pages for a small consultancy
excerpt: Show the constraint, the decision the buyer would have delayed, and the problem you take. A screenshot without that decision is decoration. End on the working session.

caption: Proof should be specific enough to choose, like titles you can read. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should open a consultancy proof page?
faqs.answer: State the constraint, the decision, and the problem. The decision needs a verb and a cost, and it should be a choice the client would have delayed. The problem should use the same words as the homepage so a buyer can tell the story matches their stuck work.

faqs.question: Can the page omit the client's name?
faqs.answer: Yes. Keep the problem, the company shape, and the decision, and drop the brand. If the client will not allow the decision to be told, you have a logo rather than a proof page. Do not invent a result to replace the decision.

faqs.question: How should the story end?
faqs.answer: Tell a similar buyer how to book a working session: what to bring, what they leave with, and what you will not turn the hour into. One action is enough. Do not end by asking them to share their journey.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A small consultancy case study page should show a buyer who might do the work themselves three things: the constraint, the decision, and the problem you actually take. A screenshot with no decision is decoration. End on how a similar buyer can book a working session. The Princeton GEO paper, by Aggarwal, Murahari, and colleagues, found that adding citations, quotations, and statistics raised source visibility by over 40 percent on their benchmark. A proof page of moods and logos gives a person nothing to quote, and it gives a DIY buyer no reason to stop doing the work alone.

Write the page so a stranger can retell the decision. If they can only retell that the client was pleased, you have written a compliment. The decision has to be one the buyer would have delayed. That delay is the comparison. If they would have made the same call on a Tuesday night, they do not need you.

## Constraint, decision, and the problem

Open with the constraint in two sentences. What was stuck, and why it was easy to postpone. A founder-led company had four price lists and used none of them. Every deal was rewritten by the founder. The team had a deck that described "value" and a spreadsheet that contradicted it. Pick the facts that made the work a decision rather than a preference. Leave the rest in the file.

Then the decision, with a verb and a cost. You refused to add a fifth price "for the strategic account." You insisted the founder pick one list before the session ended. You stopped the meeting when the room wanted more research instead of a number. "We aligned stakeholders" has no cost. A refusal does.

Then the problem, in the same words as the homepage. If this story is a pricing decision, say pricing in the first screen. A buyer is pattern-matching their own postponed work. A flattering story about a different problem teaches them this firm is a generalist, which is the industry-list failure in narrative form. Put that story on its own page or do not publish it.

Do not open with praise. Praise can close the page only if it names the decision. "They sent the price list the next morning without rewriting it" is praise with a decision inside it. "A true partner" is not.

## The decision they would have delayed

This is the part a recruiting proof does not need, and a consultancy proof does. Show the week the client would have waited. They had the data. They had the meeting. They had not chosen. Your work was the choice, made in the room, with a cost they had been avoiding. If the story is that you produced a thorough analysis and they later decided, you have described a document they could have commissioned from a freelancer, or written themselves. Move the decision into the story, or do not publish it.

Name what they gave up. A discount they liked giving. A product line they were fond of. A meeting they had to cancel because the founder was no longer required. Cost is what makes the decision believable to someone who has been hesitating for a quarter. Without a cost, the story reads as taste.

Nielsen Norman Group's research is the reason to put that cost in the first screen. People often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and they read only about a quarter of the words on a page they do visit. If the delay and the decision are below a logo and a portrait, they will not reach them. The opening is the proof. The rest is for the person who recognized their own delay.

## Why a screenshot is not a case

A slide, a blurred dashboard, or a wall of sticky notes does not show a decision. It shows that a workshop happened. Use a picture only when the picture is the decision. The one price list, with the rejected columns struck through. The sentence they would put on the homepage, with the old sentence beside it. If you cannot show the artifact, describe it in two sentences. Description beats a blurred rectangle.

Do not use a photograph of people smiling in a tasteful room. That picture is the industry list as interior design. It claims a mood. The buyer who might do this themselves is not short of mood. They are short of a choice. If a person is in the frame, they should be with the artifact, and you should have permission.

Write alt text as if the image failed. "A one-page price list with two of four columns crossed out" carries the proof. "Team collaboration" carries nothing. Do not hide a keyword in the description. The scene is the point.

## What you may tell

You can change the client's name and keep the decision. A reader does not need the brand to learn that you will not leave a room with six priorities. They need the problem, the company shape, and the cost. "A founder-led product company" is enough. "A leading innovator" is fog.

Agree the boundary before you design the page. If they will not allow the decision to be told, you have a logo, not a proof. Thank them and wait. Do not invent an outcome. The GEO finding about statistics is not a license to mint a percentage. If you know they used the price list for a season, and you may say so, say so, and say how you know. If you do not know, stop at the decision.

Read the draft as the client would, and as a competitor would. A small market can be identified from details you thought were generic. Cut those details. Keep the choice.

## What you will not claim

A proof page for this buyer fails when it borrows the language of a transformation. "We redefined the category." "We unlocked growth." Those sentences have no artifact and no cost. The buyer who has been doing the work themselves has written sentences like that in their own deck and not believed them. Match their skepticism. If the only true outcome is that one list went out and the founder stopped rewriting it, that is the outcome. Do not inflate it into a market shift you cannot show.

Also refuse a before-and-after that is only visual. A prettier document is not a decision. If the before was a mess and the after is a tidy mess, say what choice the tidy version contains. The GEO paper's point about concrete statistics is useful here only when the figure is the decision: one list, not four. A percentage with no method is the inflation you just cut.

Read the draft and highlight every sentence that would still be true if the session had not forced a choice. Delete those sentences. What remains is the proof. If too little remains, you do not have a page yet. Wait for a session you can tell.

## How the page should end

The last section is for the buyer who recognized their delay. Tell them how to book a similar session. What to bring: the artifact they have been rewriting, and the person who can say yes. What they will leave with. What you will not do: turn the session into a proposal for more research.

One action. "Book a session on this problem." The scheduler or form should know which proof they came from, so your reply can refer to the same decision. Do not end by asking them to share their journey. The session asks them to bring the postponed choice. That is the commercial point.

If the fee shape matters, one sentence can name it. Do not paste the pricing page under every story. The story's job is the decision they would have delayed.

## How many stories, and in what order to draft

Two or three stories are enough if each contains a decision someone would have postponed. Ten happy clients are a brochure. Publish stories that match the offers. If you have no story for an offer, do not invent one. Leave the offer up only when the outcome and boundary are already clear.

Date the work, or say it was within the last two years if a date would identify the client. Undated proof feels reusable from a previous firm. Remove a story when the method has changed.

Give each story its own address and a title that names the problem and the decision. "Case study" does not say which delay the page is about. "A pricing session where we refused a fifth list" does.

Draft in this order, before layout. The constraint. The decision and its cost. The problem in homepage language. What you will not disclose. The session a similar buyer should book. Read it to someone who was not in the room. If they cannot say what was refused, and why the client would have waited, the proof is still missing. Add that. Do not add adjectives.

Only then choose a picture. If it does not show the artifact or the cost, it does not go on the page.

When the story can be retold, the buyer still has to find it. Read [how the navigation should name the problem, not the department](/blog/navigation-for-a-small-consultancy) so the proof sits on a path they already understand.

If you want help turning a postponed decision into a page someone can quote, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the constraint and the cost. Leave the compliments in the draft you are willing to cut.
